title: Designing for Multi-sensory Experiences in the Built Environment
research_question: What type of experiences should be designed for the built environment? How can multi-sensory design provide a systematic approach to design for experiences?

participants.description: Healthy students, used to technology, moderately heterogeneous (mostly European and Asian people), interaction design students (for questionnaire), university students (for usability test).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies convenience sampling from university students.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Urban environment, elevator context (museum elevator, company facilities elevator), new media panel UI prototype, music in elevator (blindfolded condition), architectural structure, vending machine, airport restroom, train interface.

measures.instrument: WhatsApp design probe (media + text), questionnaire (adjectives, reasons for emotions), user observations
Usability test observation (recorded with action cameras)
Affinity diagram themes (attractiveness, efficiency, sense of control, coherence, stimulation, novelty)
Self-report (descriptions of feelings evoked by music)
Self-report (ease of use, understanding what will happen)

findings.antecedent: factors that affect user experience quality in the built environment
findings.mechanism: Six main themes identified: attractiveness, coherence, novelty, stimulation, feeling of control, and sense of efficiency.
findings.quote: This thesis identified six main themes related to factors that affect user experience quality in the built environment.

limitations: Close collaboration with a company and deep involvement in the research project may affect participant's mindset, analysis, and outcome results, potentially compromising objectivity.
Verbal content from the design probe remained somewhat poor.
Questionnaires involved conscious reflection from participants, which might alter the original experience.
User observation focused more on system usability, which was not the most relevant issue for the research.

Research participants were healthy students, used to technology, and mostly European/Asian, which may limit generalizability to other user groups (e.g., those critical of new technology, or with sensory disabilities).
The museum elevator was a secondary transport method, and architecture guided users to stairs primarily, potentially affecting elevator experience.
The study did not weigh the importance of sensory signals or define which are strongest.
The study did not suggest what type of sensory signals should be used more.
The multi-sensory user journey map does not define the intensity or importance of individual signals.
The map includes a node of co-experience but does not focus on it, as research focused on personal UX and did not yield notable co-experience insights.
The multi-sensory user journey map was not tested or evaluated in a real setting within the scope of the thesis.

paper_metadata.title: The temporal representation of experience in subjective mood
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The temporal representation of experience in subjective mood
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Humans refer to their mood state regularly in day-to-day as well as clinical interactions. Theoretical accounts suggest that when reporting on our mood we integrate over the history of our experiences; yet, the temporal structure of this integration remains unexamined. Here, we use a computational approach to quantitatively answer this question and show that early events exert a stronger influence on reported mood (a primacy weighting) compared to recent events. We show that a Primacy model accounts better for mood reports compared to a range of alternative temporal representations across random, consistent, or dynamic reward environments, different age groups, and in both healthy and depressed participants. Moreover, we find evidence for neural encoding of the Primacy, but not the Recency, model in frontal brain regions related to mood regulation. These findings hold implications for the timing of events in experimental or clinical settings and suggest new directions for individualized mood interventions.

crossref_abstract: Humans refer to their mood state regularly in day-to-day as well as clinical interactions. Theoretical accounts suggest that when reporting on our mood we integrate over the history of our experiences; yet, the temporal structure of this integration remains unexamined. Here, we use a computational approach to quantitatively answer this question and show that early events exert a stronger influence on reported mood (a primacy weighting) compared to recent events. We show that a Primacy model accounts better for mood reports compared to a range of alternative temporal representations across random, consistent, or dynamic reward environments, different age groups, and in both healthy and depressed participants. Moreover, we find evidence for neural encoding of the Primacy, but not the Recency, model in frontal brain regions related to mood regulation. These findings hold implications for the timing of events in experimental or clinical settings and suggest new directions for individualized mood interventions.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments restore directed attention; this paper explores how built environments can be designed to achieve similar restorative effects through multi-sensory design.
Exposure to natural environments reduces physiological stress; this paper investigates how multi-sensory design in built environments can contribute to stress reduction.
Environments offer opportunities for action (affordances) that are perceived directly through sensory information, influencing user experience.
Cognition and experience are shaped by the body's interaction with the environment, highlighting the importance of multi-sensory engagement.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that congruent and harmonious multi-sensory inputs in the built environment lead to enhanced cognitive processing, positive affective states, and ultimately, improved user experience quality.

steps.from_construct: Multi-sensory congruence/harmony (e.g., visual, auditory, tactile alignment)

steps.to_construct: Reduced cognitive load / Enhanced processing fluency
